content: 1. Administration of 1 gram of ceftriaxone or a consolidated 24-hour dose of an aminoglycoside is recommended for certain conditions. 2. For patients requiring hospitalization due to high fever, elevated white blood cell count, vomiting, dehydration, or evidence of sepsis, the preferred treatment regimen includes intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Options include a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside with or without ampicillin, an extended-spectrum cephalosporin or penicillin with or without an aminoglycoside, or a carbapenem. The choice of agent should be guided by local resistance data and tailored based on susceptibility results. Sterile Pyuria 3. Pyuria is defined as the presence of 10 or more white blood cells per cubic millimeter in a urine specimen, 3 or more white blood cells per high-power field in unspun urine, a positive Gram stain of unspun urine, or a positive urinary dipstick test for leukocyte esterase. 4. Sterile pyuria refers to the persistent presence of white blood cells in the urine without detectable bacteria, as determined by aerobic culture techniques on 5% sheep-blood agar and MacConkey agar plates. 5. Bacteriuria is defined as bacterial colony counts exceeding 1,000 colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter in urine. Causes of Sterile Pyuria 6. Infectious causes include gynecologic infections, urethritis caused by Chlamydia, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma, or Ureaplasma, prostatitis, balanitis, appendicitis, viral infections of the lower genitourinary tract, genitourinary tuberculosis, fungal infections, and parasitic diseases such as trichomoniasis or schistosomiasis. 7. Non-infectious causes include current antibiotic use, recent treatment of a urinary tract infection (within the past 2 weeks), presence or recent use of a urinary catheter, recent cystoscopy or urologic endoscopy, urinary tract stones, foreign bodies such as surgical mesh or retained stents, urinary tract neoplasms, pelvic irradiation, urinary fistula, polycystic kidney disease, renal transplant rejection, renal vein thrombosis, interstitial nephritis or analgesic nephropathy, papillary necrosis, interstitial cystitis, and inflammatory diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or Kawasaki disease. Pathogen-Directed Antimicrobial Therapy 8. For tuberculosis, the preferred regimen includes isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 3–6 months. 9. For gonorrhea, the preferred regimen is a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg, followed by either azithromycin 1 gram orally in a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. 10. For chlamydia, the preferred regimen is azithromycin 1 gram orally in a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. An alternative regimen includes erythromycin base 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days. 11. For Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma infections, the preferred regimen includes azithromycin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin. 12. For genital herpes, the preferred regimen includes acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days, acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 7–10 days, famciclovir 250 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days, or valacyclovir 1 gram orally twice daily for 7 days. 13. For trichomoniasis, the preferred regimen is metronidazole 2 grams orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 grams orally in a single dose. 14. For fungal infections, the preferred regimen includes fluconazole, posaconazole, echinocandins, or amphotericin B. 15. For schistosomiasis, the preferred regimen is praziquantel 20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 1–2 days. Syphilis 16. For primary and secondary syphilis in non-HIV-infected adults, the preferred regimen is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50,000 units/kg (up to 2.4 million units) intramuscularly in a single dose. 17. For early latent syphilis, the preferred regimen is the same as for primary and secondary syphilis. 18. For late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the preferred regimen for adults is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly for three doses, each administered at one-week intervals. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50,000 units/kg (up to 2.4 million units) intramuscularly, administered as three doses at one-week intervals. 19. For tertiary syphilis, the preferred regimen is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly for three doses, each at one-week intervals. 20. For neurosyphilis, the preferred regimen is aqueous crystalline penicillin G 3–4 million units intravenously every 4 hours or continuously for 10–14 days. An alternative regimen includes procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once daily for 10–14 days, combined with probenecid 500 mg orally four times daily for 10–14 days. Syphilis in HIV-Infected Persons 21. The treatment regimens for primary, secondary, and latent syphilis in HIV-infected individuals are the same as those for non-HIV-infected individuals. Syphilis During Pregnancy 22. Pregnant women should be treated with the penicillin regimen appropriate for their stage of infection. Congenital Syphilis 23. Infants with proven or highly probable congenital syphilis and abnormal physical examination findings, a nontreponemal serologic titer fourfold higher than the mother’s titer, or a positive darkfield test of body fluids should receive aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 units/kg intravenously every 12 hours during the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter for a total of 10 days, or procaine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg intramuscularly once daily for 10 days. 24. Infants with normal physical examinations and nontreponemal serologic titers the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, but whose mothers were inadequately treated, have no documentation of treatment, were treated with erythromycin or another non-penicillin regimen, or were treated less than 4 weeks before delivery, should receive the same treatment as above. 25. Infants with normal physical examinations and nontreponemal serologic titers the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, and whose mothers were treated appropriately during pregnancy with no evidence of reinfection or relapse, should receive a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg. 26. Infants with normal physical examinations and nontreponemal serologic titers the same or less than fourfold the maternal titer, and whose mothers were adequately treated before pregnancy with stable, low nontreponemal serologic titers (VDRL <1:2; RPR <1:4) during pregnancy and at delivery, should receive aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 units/kg every 4–6 hours for 10 days. Urethritis 27. For nongonococcal urethritis, the preferred regimen is azithromycin 1 gram orally in a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. 28. Alternative regimens include erythromycin base 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days, erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg orally four times daily for 7 days, or levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days.
